Spotting Crops in Radar Images Without Cleaning the Noise First

A plain-language rewrite of "Speckle aware spatial search based segmentation algorithm for crop classification in SAR images using a three component K-NN model" by Chandran Bipin, Chandu Venkateswara Rao and Padavala Veera Sridevi (Journal of Applied Remote Sensing, Vol. 17(4), 2023).

Original paper: C. Bipin, C. V. Rao and P. V. Sridevi, "Speckle aware spatial search based segmentation algorithm for crop classification in SAR images using a three component K-NN model," J. Appl. Remote Sens. 17(4), 048503 (2023), doi:10.1117/1.JRS.17.048503. Bracketed numbers like [4] point to the reference list at the end and follow the original paper's numbering.

Summary (Abstract)

The authors built a method for sorting radar satellite images into regions, such as different crops. Radar images are grainy with a type of noise called speckle. Instead of cleaning that noise away first, their method treats it as one of the things it expects to see. Each feature in the image is described by three "components," and the method grows regions outward from confident starting points using a simple machine learning technique called K-NN. They tried it on Sentinel-1 satellite data and compared it with K-NN applied after four popular noise filters (Lee, Refined Lee, Frost and Gamma-MAP). Their method classified crops more accurately than all of them.

1. Introduction

Plenty of jobs, like tracking floods or crops, need satellite pictures at regular intervals. Radar satellites (SAR) are good for this because they are dependable, work in any weather, and are relatively cheap. They send out their own microwave signal, so they don't need sunlight, and the signal passes through clouds, rain and haze. Regular optical satellites struggle in those conditions.

Radar has its downsides too. It sends a signal at one narrow frequency and records what bounces back. This process creates a grainy noise called speckle. Optical images, which capture many colors, don't suffer from it. Radar also lacks color information, so all you have to work with are the available polarizations (the orientation of the radio waves). All of this makes radar images harder to read than ordinary photos.

One common fix is to blend radar images with optical ones. But in the very situations where radar matters most, like floods or monsoon-season crops, the optical images are blocked by clouds. So we need methods that work from radar alone.

This paper tests whether a "region-growing" approach can pick out different crops in radar data, while accounting for speckle and using two polarizations. The authors describe a way of representing a feature and its speckle using three levels, and compare it with the usual approach of filtering first and classifying afterwards.

Region-growing means picking a starting pixel and repeatedly adding neighboring pixels that look similar. It works well on noisy radar images because it can follow the edges of a feature even when the picture is grainy.[1][2] Many versions of this idea exist.[3]

A previous method by the same group, called search-based image analysis (SBIA), used this idea to find water bodies in radar images.[4] It represented water using three levels and searched outward from starting points. One level handled speckle (with a limit on how big a speckle spot can be), one marked the confident "seed" pixels, and one covered the bulk of the water. The levels were set by trying many values.

That earlier method only worked for a few kinds of features because it relied on fixed thresholds tuned for water. It did give results that tolerated speckle, but it then needed extra custom steps, like removing shadows and using polarization checks, to tell water apart from look-alikes.

To make it work for more kinds of features, it has to use both polarizations. A well-known alternative is polarimetric decomposition, which works out what kind of surface the signal bounced off, based on physics.[5][6] But that normally needs "full" or "hybrid" polarimetric data[7], which is expensive in terms of satellite power. Sentinel-1 gives only dual-polarization data over land, so that route is closed.

Speckle isn't unique to radar. Any imaging technique built on coherent waves, such as lasers or ultrasound, has it. It comes from the nature of coherent imaging,[8] depends on the instrument's settings, and acts multiplicatively, so ordinary linear smoothing doesn't remove it well.[9][10][11]

The usual solution is a set of special non-linear filters: Lee[12], Refined Lee[13], Frost[14] and Gamma-MAP[15]. They are popular because they smooth noise while keeping edges, adjusting to whether a patch looks like an edge or a flat area. Many studies compare them.[16][17]

In this paper, the fixed thresholds from the old method are swapped for a K-NN classifier working on two-dimensional points (VV and VH values). K-NN is a simple and widely used method that labels something based on its nearest labeled neighbors.[18] The old three-level model becomes a three-component model, and it is combined with region growing.

Microwaves have longer wavelengths than visible light and can reach deeper into plant canopies, which gives more information about what type of plant it is and how it is growing.[19][20][21][22]

So the new method, SBIA-KNN, replaces the threshold-based model with the K-NN-based three-component model. That removes the need for a de-speckling filter before processing, and lets the method extract features from radar data alone.

The data come from the European Space Agency's Sentinel-1 satellites, part of the Copernicus program. They carry C-band radar, give global coverage, have 10 m resolution, and revisit about every 12 days near the equator.[23] The data are free through Sentinel Hub[24] and are useful for disaster management, land planning and environmental monitoring. This paper uses the dual-polarization data.

In short, the paper presents a region-growing method with a three-component model built on K-NN, tests it on farmland to classify crops, and compares the results with filter-based classification.

2. Methodology

The overall process is in Figure 1. In training, labeled sample points are used to build a basic two-class K-NN classifier (feature versus background). The confidence scores from that classifier are used to build the three-component model. At evaluation time, the method repeatedly searches through the image using that model. To check it fairly, the same image is also filtered with the common filters and classified with ordinary K-NN, and the results are compared against SBIA-KNN.

Plants scatter microwaves throughout their volume. How much energy comes back, and with what polarization, depends on how dense, tall and wet the canopy is. Denser canopies scatter more, and wetter plants scatter more than dry ones. Together these give each type of vegetation its own "signature," which can be used to tell crops apart and judge how much vegetation there is.

The three-component model describes a feature in the radar data like this:

  • Component 1: pixels that clearly and unmistakably belong to the feature. These become the starting seeds.
  • Component 2: the bulk of the feature. These pixels can look similar to another class, so a component-2 patch only counts if it touches at least one component-1 patch.
  • Component 3: the areas most badly messed up by speckle. They are very likely to be misclassified and are basically unpredictable. They show up as small spots scattered across the feature.[4]

2.1 Search Based Image Analysis

A "search" starts at a seed pixel and spreads to its neighbors. A classifier decides which neighbors get the same label as the seed. It keeps going until no more connected pixels qualify. Algorithm 1 gives the step-by-step version for a scene, a three-component model and a starting point.

Algorithm 1: Search (S, M, p0, li)
WorkList     ← [p0]
ResultList   ← ∅
NeighborList ← ∅
History      ← ∅
while WorkList ≠ ∅ do
    pt ← POP(WorkList)
    if pt ∉ History then
        if M(pt) = li then
            PUSH(ResultList, pt)
            Neighbors = N_S(pt)
            APPEND(WorkList, Neighbors)
        else
            PUSH(NeighborList, pt)
        end if
        PUSH(History, pt)
    end if
    if li = 3 then
        if len(WorkList) ≥ MaxSpeckle then
            ResultList   ← ∅
            NeighborList ← ∅
            return ResultList, NeighborList
        end if
    end if
end while
return ResultList, NeighborList

In plain terms: keep a to-do list of pixels, starting with the seed. Take one pixel off the list; if it has the label we're searching for, keep it and add its neighbors to the to-do list, otherwise remember it as an "other" neighbor. Never visit a pixel twice. For speckle (component 3), give up and throw away the result if the to-do list grows beyond MaxSpeckle.

In the algorithm, the neighbor function simply lists the pixels around a given pixel, and "MaxSpeckle" is the largest size a speckle spot is expected to be inside a feature.

One search collects all the connected pixels with the same component label. Pixels that don't match are saved as unvisited neighbors. These can then be used as new seeds for further searches with their own labels. For component 3, a search is stopped and thrown out if it grows beyond the MaxSpeckle size, since a real speckle spot should be small.

All the pixels collected in one search form an image object, or "parcel." Algorithm 2 runs these searches in a nested way across all components in a scene. Each search belongs to a single feature, so you need separate three-component models to classify several different features in an area.

Algorithm 2: Multicomponent search (S, K-NN, p0)
WorkList   ← [p0]
ResultList ← ∅
while WorkList ≠ ∅ do
    pt ← POP(WorkList)
    li ← k-nn(pt)
    Result, Neighbors ← Search(S, k-nn, pt, li)
    APPEND(ResultList, Result)
    APPEND(WorkList, Neighbors)
end while
return ResultList

In plain terms: take a pixel, ask the K-NN model which component it belongs to, run Algorithm 1 from there, then use the leftover "other" neighbors as new starting points, until nothing is left to search.

A search only spreads within the region covered by its feature. To cover a whole area, you need to start searches from several suitable seed points. Also, one feature can end up with several labels.

2.2 Estimation of the Three-Component Model

K-NN is a supervised learning method that can be used for classification or regression. First, a two-class K-NN is trained on randomly picked labeled points from the feature and from its background (Equation 1: a point is labeled "feature" if it belongs to the feature, otherwise "background").

K-NN classifies a point by looking at its k closest labeled points and taking the majority. The "prediction probability" is simply the fraction of those k neighbors that are labeled as the feature (Equation 2).

Next, another random set of labeled points is scored with this two-class model, and the points are sorted into three groups by score (Equations 3 to 6): the highest scores go to component 1, the lowest to component 3, and everything in between to component 2.

(1) L2(p) = { lf  if p ∈ feature;  lbg  otherwise }

A point gets the "feature" label if it belongs to the feature, and the "background" label otherwise.

(2) Pknn(p) = (1/k) · Σnni ∈ NNp [ L2(nni) = lf ]

The prediction probability is the share of a point's k nearest neighbors, NNp = {nn1, nn2, …, nnk}, that are labeled as the feature.

(3) L3(x) = { l1 | x ∈ X1;  l2 | x ∈ X2;  l3 | x ∈ X3 }

Each point is given one of three labels depending on which of the three sets it falls into.

(4) X1 = { xi | Pknn(xi) > Pknn(yj)  ∀ yj ∈ X2 }

Component 1: points with a higher score than every component-2 point (the most confident ones).

(5) X2 = { xi | Pknn(zk) < Pknn(xi) < Pknn(yj)  ∀ yj, zk ∈ X3, X1 }

Component 2: points scoring between the component-3 points and the component-1 points (the bulk of the feature).

(6) X3 = { xi | Pknn(xi) < Pknn(yj)  ∀ yj ∈ X2 }

Component 3: points with a lower score than every component-2 point (the ones most hit by speckle).

A new K-NN model is then built from the component-1 and component-3 points (plus the middle group), so that it can assign any point to one of the three classes.

The size of each group is flexible. Keeping component 1 small compared to the other two means fewer seed points, and so fewer searches needed to finish the job. But if it is too small, some feature segments will be missed altogether.

3. Data and Model Preparation

SBIA is meant to be general and should work for many features and datasets. Here the authors test it on separating crops in Sentinel-1 data.

Sentinel-1 collects C-band radar data at regular 12-day intervals.[23] They picked farmland near Illinois (around 41.110° N, 90.36° W), from a satellite pass on May 31, 2021. The data are free from the Copernicus open access hub,[24] and the area has many large agricultural fields. The data were prepared for terrain correction and calibration using ESA's SNAP software.

The two polarizations, VV and VH, were stacked into a false-color image, with VV as the red band and VH as the green band.

The authors looked through the image by eye and chose an area with three clearly different color patterns. These could be three different crops, or the same crop at different growth stages. The data for this area are in Figure 2(a).

Figure 2(b) shows the labeled areas. Three crops (or growth stages) were identified by hand from the false-color image, with at least two patches for each.

For each crop, a three-component model was built from random points taken from its area. The points were split into components 1, 2 and 3 in a 1:8:8 ratio. A speckle size of 200 pixels was used in the search.

SBIA with this model was then used to segment the area. The best model used 1500 points and k = 15 neighbors. To find seeds, the image was first classified with the three-component model, and pixels labeled component 1 were used as seeds. A search was started from every seed.

For comparison, the image was filtered with a Lee filter (3×3 and 5×5 windows), with Frost and Gamma-MAP filters (5×5), and with a Refined Lee filter. K-NN models were trained on the filtered data and used to classify it. All results were checked against the hand-labeled areas.

The authors also wanted to know what happens if you filter the data before using SBIA. They used the 5×5 Lee-filtered data to build the three-component model and ran SBIA on it. Figure 3 shows how the three labels are spread out in the VV-VH plot. In 3(a) (unfiltered data), the component-1 points from each crop are well separated, but components 2 and 3 overlap a lot with the other crops. In 3(b) (Lee-filtered data), the overlap between crops drops considerably and only remains in component 3.

To check how reliable the method is and find the best settings, the authors ran a parameter sweep, varying the model size (number of points in the K-NN model) and k (number of neighbors). For each setting they built ten models using different random draws, and recorded the average accuracy and its spread. The results are in Table 2.

4. Results

Figure 4(a) shows the SBIA-KNN result. Visually, speckle has much less effect on the segmented image. Accuracy was measured against the reference areas in Figure 2(b). The result of plain K-NN on unfiltered data is in Figure 4(b).

Results for K-NN on filtered data (Lee 3×3, Lee 5×5, Frost 5×5, Gamma-MAP 5×5) are in Figures 4(c) to 4(f).

Filtered results keep edges neat, whereas SBIA's edges come out rough and uneven. But SBIA cuts down false detections a lot. Figure 5 shows the confusion matrix for each experiment (a table showing which crops got mistaken for which), and Table 1 lists precision, recall, F1 score[25] and overall accuracy. Overall, SBIA beats the conventional approach.

Comparing plain SBIA (Fig. 4a) with SBIA on filtered data (Fig. 4h), the filter doesn't help much inside the validation areas. Outside those areas, though, pre-filtering avoids a lot of probable false detections. The authors suggest this is because filtering squeezes the feature points closer together, as seen in Figure 3(b).

The parameter sweep in Table 2 shows that the method gives a steady average accuracy of about 86% with a model size of 1500 and k = 15, with the spread in accuracy under 2%. That setting was chosen as the best for this area and these crops.

4.1 Conclusion

The paper extends the earlier search-based method so it can handle general features in radar images, using the three-component K-NN model. This lets it detect a range of targets. It improves accuracy by roughly 20% over ordinary K-NN on unfiltered data, and it also beats K-NN on data cleaned by the popular de-speckling filters. Speckle still affects the boundaries of features, but inside the segmented regions its effect is much smaller than in the unfiltered result (Fig. 4b). The processing time depends on the data.

The algorithm doesn't care about shape or orientation. It is expected to do poorly on messy, mixed areas like cities, where buildings and plants sit together. The three-component model also doesn't help much when the target is very small.

The authors say the method could be used with other coherent imaging sources, like ultrasound and laser imaging, and could be combined with other machine learning methods besides K-NN.

Code and Data Availability

The code is on GitHub at github.com/vu3bpn/sbia_knn. The input data can be downloaded from Sentinel Hub using the pass date and location given in the paper.

About the Authors

Chandran Bipin is a former research fellow at the National Remote Sensing Centre, Hyderabad, and is working toward a PhD at Andhra University College of Engineering, Visakhapatnam. His master's degree in electronics engineering is from Cochin University of Science and Technology.

Chandu Venkateswara Rao is a former scientist at the National Remote Sensing Centre (ISRO), Hyderabad. He earned an ME in digital systems from Osmania University in 1985 and a PhD in computer science and engineering from JNTU Hyderabad in 2009. He works on image fusion, combining data across space and time, and classifying satellite images.

Padavala Veera Sridevi studied at Acharya Nagarjuna University (undergraduate, 1986), PSG College of Technology (postgraduate, 1988) and Andhra University (PhD, 1997). She is a professor in the Electronics and Communication Engineering department at Andhra University College of Engineering (professor since 2013) and was Head of that department at the university's women's engineering college from 2010 to 2013. Her interests include antennas, electromagnetics and VLSI.
